title: client — the Blazor WebAssembly reader and world map

overview.l1: This folder is the whole browser app the reader actually uses: the KJV reading page, the /world time-and-place map, and every popover, picker, and hover card that lets you click a verse, a place, or an event and jump somewhere else in the graph. It runs entirely in the browser (Blazor WebAssembly compiles C# to run client-side, like a second engine alongside JavaScript) and talks to the Rust server only over plain HTTP GET requests. If this folder vanished there would be no way to read Scripture or see the map at all — the server would still hold all the data, but nothing would render it.
overview.l2: Program.cs wires up dependency injection (DI — a container that hands each class the collaborators it needs instead of it constructing them itself) at startup: it registers AtlasClient and GraphExplorableClient (the two HTTP ports to the server), the state atoms (client/State/), the view registry (client/Views/), and localStorage-backed services. IExplorableClient/GraphExplorableClient is the generic 'ask the graph a question' port — Card/Edges/Reading — used alongside the older, bespoke AtlasClient. client/Explore/ holds the 'exploration model': one C# class per node kind (VerseNode, PlaceNode, EventNode, …) implementing IExplorable, plus the registry of popover-section providers that assemble a node's popover body. client/State/ holds the state-atom layer (compiled contracts in client/Contracts/State.cs) — named, typed stores like Locus and TimeWindow that components read as projections and write only via typed intents, so two panes showing 'the same chapter' can never silently disagree. client/Components/ is the reusable UI: verse rendering, the shared ExplorerPopover, the map's PlaceCard/TimeSlider, and the split-view host. client/Pages/ are the routed pages (Reader at '/', World at '/world', Kretzmann, Concord, Sources) and client/Layout/MainLayout.razor is the shared header/hamburger chrome every page renders inside.
overview.l3: Dependency direction, outside in: Pages/*.razor mount Components/*.razor, which push/pop Explore/*.cs IExplorable nodes through a shared ExplorerPopover (client/Components/ExplorerPopover.razor), whose body is assembled by PopoverSectionRegistry.Providers (client/Explore/PopoverSections.cs:230) — an ordered list of IPopoverSectionProvider instances (client/Explore/PopoverSectionProviders.cs, 3128 lines, 28 provider classes) that each answer 'does this node kind have content for my section' and resolve it against AtlasClient/IExplorableClient. Shared, cross-page facts (the current locus, the active time window, the view arrangement, the selection tray) live in StateAtom<T> singletons (client/State/StateAtom.cs) registered in Program.cs/AppServices.cs and read through Projection<T> (client/State/Projection.cs) — the compiled contract in client/Contracts/State.cs enforces single-writer, idempotence, no-echo, confluence and agreement, each with its own property test in client.Tests. client/Contracts/{Views,Focus,Frontier,Interactions,State}.cs is the 'compiled authority' the 2026-08-26 frontend-backend-contract-design spec names: IView/IViewComponent/IViewComposition (composition, never inheritance), IFocusComponent/IFrontierAbstraction/ITraversal/IEscapeHatch (the Focus/Frontier/Traversal/EscapeHatch vocabulary), IInteractionContract (the closed Hover/Click/CtrlClick/ShiftClick/Highlight gesture set), and IStateAtom/IStateLink/IStateEffect. client/Views/ViewRegistry.cs realizes IViewComposition over the live ViewArrangement atom; CompositionSplit.razor is the one place every host page (Reader, World, Sources, Kretzmann, Concord) gets its split-pane machinery from, so a host declares almost nothing of its own. Server communication is entirely GET-based JSON over Wire.Options (client/Wire.cs) — snake_case to match the server's serde output — through two clients: AtlasClient (client/AtlasClient.cs, per-endpoint LRU caches for hot hover paths) for the bespoke '/api/*' surface, and GraphExplorableClient (client/GraphExplorableClient.cs) implementing IExplorableClient for the three generic graph endpoints (node card, edge page, text window). App.razor gates the whole app on an AQC (Atlas Query Contract) version check against '/api/contract' before rendering the Router at all, per the design spec's fail-loud versioning law.

files.role: The app's entry point: wires every DI service before the app renders anything.
files.l1: This is the very first C# code that runs when the page loads. It builds the app, tells it where the HTML page mounts (the '#app' div), and registers every shared service the rest of the app depends on: the HTTP clients that talk to the server, the shared 'where am I in Scripture / what time window is the map showing' state, and the registry of pages that can be split side by side. If this file were missing, nothing else would ever be handed the objects it needs to run.
files.l2: `WebAssemblyHostBuilder.CreateDefault` builds the host; `builder.Services.Add*` calls register everything else as **dependency injection** (DI) — a pattern where a class declares what it needs in its constructor and a container supplies it, rather than the class constructing its own dependencies. `AddSingleton` means one shared instance for the app's whole life (Blazor WebAssembly has exactly one DI scope, so 'singleton' and 'scoped' mean the same thing here). It registers `AtlasClient` and `IExplorableClient` (each with its own `HttpClient`), `ViewStateService`, the state atoms via `AppServices.AddStateAtoms`/`AddSelectionAtom`, `EffectRegistry` (bound to both its concrete type and its interface), `OwnershipRegistry`, `SavedExplorationsService` (localStorage-backed), and the `ViewRegistry` built by `ViewRegistrySetup.Build`. The final line, `await builder.Build().RunAsync()`, actually starts the app.
files.l3: `AtlasClient` and `IExplorableClient`/`GraphExplorableClient` (line ~17-32) each get their own `HttpClient`, deliberately not sharing one — see `GraphExplorableClient`'s own header for why. State atoms are split into two registration calls (`AppServices.AddStateAtoms`/`AddSelectionAtom`, line 63/84) specifically so `client.Tests` can exercise real DI resolution and singleton lifetime, rather than text-scanning this file (a prior approach that could only prove a constructor call appears somewhere, never registration or lifetime). `EffectRegistry` is bound under both its concrete type and `IEffectRegistry` to the same instance (line 71-72) so callers needing `EffectClaim.ReconcileTask` avoid a downcast. `ViewRegistrySetup.Build` (line 100) closes over already-registered singletons (`StateAtom<ViewArrangement>`, `ViewStateService`, `StateAtom<Locus>`, `NavigationManager`) — no live component instance is needed to build the registry. No dedicated unit test; correctness of registration/lifetime is asserted by `client.Tests`' conformance suite against `AppServices`, not this file directly.

Program.cs calls both methods directly — this is not a parallel copy that could drift, it is the only implementation. files.role: The root component: gates the whole app on a server contract-version check before routing.
files.l1: This is the very first thing rendered on screen. Before showing the reader or the map, it asks the server 'what versions of our shared contract do you support' and compares that to the version this build of the app was compiled against. If they don't match, it shows a plain error page instead of the app — a mismatched deploy should fail loudly, not quietly serve broken data.
files.l2: `OnInitializedAsync` calls `Api.Contract()` (a `Task<ContractDto>`) with a 2-second cancellation timeout. A network failure, timeout, or unparseable JSON is treated as **not** a version mismatch (the check exists to catch deployment skew, not general connectivity) and the app proceeds normally. A parseable-but-out-of-range version — checked via `AqcContract.Satisfies` — sets `_state` to `Mismatch`, and the markup swaps in `<ContractMismatch>` instead of the ordinary `<Router>`. `_state` is a small private enum (`Checking`/`Ok`/`Mismatch`) driving a `@switch` in the markup.
files.l3: `AqcContract.Satisfies` throwing `FormatException` (a malformed advertised range) is caught separately from the network-failure catch (line 60) and routed to `Mismatch`, not silently swallowed — a real fix-round correction: a malformed advertisement is precisely the deployment-skew case this gate exists for. `CheckTimeout` (2s) bounds how long first paint can be blocked by an unreachable `/api/contract`. Tested by `tests/ux/contract-versioning.spec.ts` (Playwright) covering both the malformed-response and timeout paths.

files.role: The one JsonSerializerOptions instance every HTTP (de)serialization uses.
files.l1: A single shared setting object that tells the app's JSON reader/writer to expect field names like `from_year` instead of `FromYear` — matching exactly how the Rust server writes its JSON. Every network request and response in this app goes through this one object, so the naming convention can never quietly drift between two call sites.
files.l2: `Wire.Options` is a `static readonly JsonSerializerOptions` with `PropertyNamingPolicy = JsonNamingPolicy.SnakeCaseLower`. Every DTO in `Dtos.cs` is deserialized against this policy (via `HttpClient.GetFromJsonAsync(url, Wire.Options)`), which is what lets `FromYear` on the C# side line up with the server's `from_year` without either side hand-writing a `[JsonPropertyName]` attribute per field.
files.l3: Using one shared `JsonSerializerOptions` instance (rather than a fresh one per call) also avoids .NET's own repeated-instantiation cost warning for that type. Consumed by `AtlasClient`, `GraphExplorableClient`, and `MapInterop` (for object payloads sent into JS, which otherwise use `IJSObjectReference.InvokeAsync`'s own camelCase default — see `MapInterop.SetScene`'s own comment for why the distinction matters). No dedicated tests; correctness is implied by every DTO round-tripping correctly in integration/Playwright coverage.

files.role: The client's own compiled AQC (Atlas Query Contract) version and the semver-range check.
files.l1: This file hard-codes which version of the client-server 'contract' this build was compiled against, and knows how to check whether the server's advertised range of supported versions includes it. It is the client half of the version check App.razor runs at startup — without it, a mismatched client and server could talk past each other silently.
files.l2: `AqcContract.ClientVersion` is a `const string` ('0.1.0') kept by hand in lockstep with `contracts/atlas-query-contract/VERSION`. `Satisfies(ContractDto)` parses the client version and the server's `MinVersion`/`MaxVersion` into `(Major, Minor, Patch)` tuples via a private `ParseSemver`, then compares with a private `Compare` helper — no external semver package, just three integers compared in order.
files.l3: `ParseSemver` throws `FormatException` on anything that isn't exactly three dot-separated integers — a deliberate fail-loud choice `App.razor` relies on to distinguish 'malformed advertisement' (a real deployment-skew signal) from 'network unreachable' (benign). `Satisfies` mirrors the Rust cucumber harness's own `satisfies` function (server: `server/atlas-server/src/contract.rs`), and `glossary.md` pairs the two as independently-implemented checks of the identical phrase. No dedicated unit test file found for this class specifically; covered indirectly by `versioning.feature` (the Gherkin contract corpus, run on both sides) and `tests/ux/contract-versioning.spec.ts`.

files.role: Every wire DTO (record) mirroring the JSON shapes atlas-server serves.
files.l1: This file is the app's phrasebook for talking to the server: one small data shape per kind of answer the server can give — a Scene (what's on the map), a ChapterOut (a chapter's verses), a VerseDetail (a verse's cross-references and events), and dozens more. If the server changed a field name here without a matching change on the server, every screen that used it would silently show nothing instead of that data — this file is the seam where that mismatch would show up first.
files.l2: Every type here is a C# `record` — an immutable data class where equality compares values, not just references — deserialized straight from JSON via `Wire.Options` (snake_case matching). Records are grouped by feature: `Scene`/`ScenePlace`/`SceneEvent`/`SceneArrow` (the map's own picture of one time window), `ChapterOut`/`VerseOut`/`HeadingDto` (the reader's chapter payload), `EventDetail`/`EventWitnessDto` (an event node's rich content), `CatechismItemDetail`, `PlaceDetail`/`PlaceHistoryOut`, `PolityEraOut` (map borders), `SourcesDocumentOut`/`ProvenanceEntryDto` (attribution), and the generic graph port's own `NodeCardDto`/`EdgePageDto`/`TextWindowDto`. Many records carry an optional trailing `Provenance`/`*Provenance` field (nullable, default-omitted) added across several batches — always additive, so older callers keep compiling unchanged.
files.l3: The doc comments on individual records are the authoritative history of several house rules: 'conditional presence' (a field is `null`/omitted rather than a fabricated placeholder — e.g. `VerseDetail.Provenance`), 'always an array, never omitted' (e.g. `Scene.QuietPlaces`), and 'no fabricated data.' `HeadingDto.Kind` ('event'|'general') backs the PRESENTATION CATEGORY LAW that lets `EventNode`/section providers render a dateless container differently from a dated one. `PolityEraOut.Rings`/`LandMaskOut.Rings` deliberately stay a raw `JsonElement` (parsed-JSON tree, no C# property names) since the client never inspects ring coordinates, only forwards them to `map.js`. `EventDetail.MentionedIn`/`Analogues`/`WitnessesProvenance`/`MentionsProvenance` are all nullable-with-`*OrEmpty` helper properties, matching the server's `skip_serializing_if` omission convention. `ContractDto` (last record, line ~1087) is the AQC version-advertisement shape `AqcContract.Satisfies` reads. No dedicated unit tests for this file itself (it is pure data); every field is exercised transitively by whichever page/component reads it, and by the Gherkin contract corpus for the generic graph DTOs.

files.role: The bespoke typed HTTP client for atlas-server's '/api/*' endpoints, with per-endpoint LRU caches.
files.l1: This is the app's main phone line to the server: every time the reader needs a chapter's text, or the map needs a scene for a time window, this class is what makes the request and hands back the parsed answer. It also remembers recent answers (up to 48 scenes, 24 chapters, and so on) so hovering the same place twice, or flipping back to a chapter you just read, is instant instead of a fresh round trip.
files.l2: One method per endpoint (`SceneTime`, `SceneScripture`, `Books`, `Eras`, `Chapter`, `Verse`, `Place`, `PlaceHistory`, `Xrefs`, `Catechism`, `CatechismItem`, `Narratives`, `NarrativeEventPositions`, `Event`, `Polities`, `Landmarks`, `LandMask`, `Sources`, `Contract`), each calling a private `GetRequired<T>` helper that does `HttpClient.GetFromJsonAsync` with `Wire.Options` and throws if the body is empty. Caching uses `LruCache<TKey,TValue>` (a fixed-capacity, least-recently-used cache — the class this file defines its own of, per endpoint) for hot, repeat-visited data (scenes, chapters, place history, xrefs, catechism spans, polities); five other endpoints (`Books`, `Eras`, `Landmarks`, `LandMask`, `Sources`) use `AsyncMemo<T>` instead — fetched once, cached forever, since that data never changes within a session.
files.l3: `ResolveBaseAddress` (a static factory method, line 75) picks the API origin from configuration's `"ApiBase"` key (dev, where the Blazor dev server and atlas-server run on different ports) or falls back to the host's own base address (release, single-binary deployment). Cache sizing is deliberate and documented per field: `_sceneCache` (capacity 48) is the hot path (one call per slider/dropdown change); `_chapterCache` (24) exists specifically because `PlaceCard`'s hover-verse-text block needs instant repeat-hover; `_placeHistoryCache`/`_xrefsCache`/`_catechismSpanCache` (all 24) mirror that reasoning. `KretzmannChapter` (line 145) is deliberately *un*cached, unlike `Chapter` — a curator-added commentary unit should be visible on the very next chapter visit, not held stale behind a cache with no invalidation path. No dedicated unit test file for `AtlasClient` itself; its shapes are pinned by the AQC Gherkin corpus and exercised end-to-end throughout `tests/ux/*.spec.ts`.

files.role: The generic 'ask the graph a question' interface — Card/Edges/Reading — and the typed EdgeKindId.
files.l1: A second, smaller phone line to the server, alongside AtlasClient — but this one speaks in generic graph terms ('give me this node's card', 'give me a page of these edges') rather than one bespoke request per screen. It exists so new kinds of content (a Person, a Kretzmann commentary item) can be fetched without the server needing a brand-new endpoint for each one.
files.l2: Declares three methods: `Card(string id)` (a node's label/kind/provenance/edge-summary), `Edges(string id, EdgeKindId kind, int? cursor, int limit)` (one page of one edge kind), and `Reading(string fromRef, int n, string dir, string corpus)` (a window along a reading spine — KJV or the Book of Concord). `EdgeKindId` is a `readonly record struct` wrapping one string, deliberately carrying no implicit conversion to/from `string` — the only way to build one is `new EdgeKindId("...")`, confined by convention to the three literal-authoring sites in `EdgeSectionRegistry.cs`.
files.l3: The `EdgeKindId` newtype closes a real risk (M-D2 Minor-2): an `id`/`kind` argument-order transposition at an `Edges` call site, which two plain `string` parameters could never let the compiler catch. `id`/`cursor` deliberately stay plain `string`/`int?` — this client represents every ref as a plain string everywhere (`VerseNode.Title` IS the vref), so a richer typed-ref hierarchy would be a second representation of the same thing. One concrete implementation ships (`GraphExplorableClient`) — per the file's own doc comment, 'where only one exists, the interface is still the only consumption path.' files.role: The Blazor<->JS bridge to the Leaflet map (map.js): pushes data in, receives events back.
files.l1: This file is the translator between C# and the actual JavaScript map library (Leaflet) that draws the world map in the browser. Every time the map needs new data — a scene's places, a set of border polygons, a landmark list — it goes through here; every time you hover or click a marker on the map, the event comes back through here too. Without it, the map would be a blank JavaScript widget with nothing on it.
files.l2: `MapInterop` is created via `MapInterop.Create`, which imports `./js/map.js` as a JS module (`IJSObjectReference`) and calls its exported `init` function, getting back an integer id for this map instance. Every other method (`SetScene`, `SetPolities`, `BeginMorph`/`MorphFrame`/`SettleMorph`, `SetLandmarks`, `SetLandMask`, `SetIsolate`, `PanToPlace`, `SetCamera`) is a thin `await _module.InvokeVoidAsync/InvokeAsync(...)` call. Events flow the other way through `IMapEvents` (an interface World.razor implements: `OnPlaceHover`, `OnPlaceClick`, `OnArrowHover`, `OnMapClick`, `OnEscapePressed`, `OnCameraChanged`, `OnPolityDeltaClick`, …) via `MapEventsSink`, a small `[JSInvokable]`-attributed wrapper class JS actually calls into (JS interop needs a concrete attributed class, not an interface).
files.l3: Object payloads sent into JS (`SetScene`, `SetPolities`, `SetLandmarks`, `SetLandMask`) are first serialized with `Wire.Options` (snake_case) into a plain string, then passed as a string argument — `IJSObjectReference.InvokeAsync`'s own default JSON serializer would rename fields to camelCase, silently diverging from what map.js is written against (documented in `SetScene`'s own comment). `SetScene` also overwrites each place's `name` key with its own `DisplayName` (the period-resolved name) before serializing, since map.js's marker-label rendering reads `p.name` directly — no map.js change needed for the Luz/Bethel name-swap feature. Two static helpers, `BlinkPlace` and `SetNarrativeFocus`, reach whichever live (non-mini) map instance(s) currently exist via map.js's own module-level `instances` registry, since their callers (a mini-reader, `ExplorerPopover`) own no `MapInterop` instance of their own. `MeasureCardPlacement` (another static helper) feeds `CardPlacement.Compute`'s flip/clamp math. No dedicated unit test file (JS interop is not unit-testable in isolation); covered by `tests/ux/*world*`/`*map*` Playwright specs.

files.role: The compiled View/ViewComponent/ViewComposition interfaces — the frontend's type-system charter.
files.l1: This file defines, as real C# interfaces, what a 'View' and a 'Composition of Views' mean in this app — a View is just 'a name, a list of components, a list of escape hatches', and a Composition (like the reader-plus-map split screen) is a View made of other Views. It exists so the owner's rule — 'no view is a privileged split host' — is something the compiler can check, not just a convention everyone has to remember.
files.l2: `IView` (name, `Components`, `EscapeHatches`) and `IViewComponent` (an empty marker interface — Blazor components implement this) are the two base shapes. `IViewComposition : IView` adds `Members` (an ordered list of `IView`) and `Layout` (`ICompositionLayout`, whose `Kind` is a plain string like `"split-h"`). files.role: The state-atom contract: IStateAtom/IProjection/IStateLink/IStateEffect and their five laws.
files.l1: This is the rulebook for how the app shares information between different pages and components — like 'what chapter is the reader currently showing' — so that two panes displaying the same fact can never quietly disagree. It says all shared facts live in one named place each (an 'atom'), nothing may write to one except through a declared change (an 'intent'), and reading one always returns the single true current value.
files.l2: `IStateAtom<T>` is one named, typed store: `Name`, `Value` (read-only from outside), `Dispatch(IIntent<T>)` (the only write path), and a `Changed` event. `IIntent<T>` is a self-describing change: a `Name` (for logging/testing), an `Origin` (`null` for a user gesture, or the name of the link that derived it — used to prevent echo loops), and `Apply(current) -> T` (must be idempotent). `IProjection<T>` is what components actually read — a thin, storage-free wrapper around a source atom. `IStateLink<A,B>` declares a derivation from one atom into another (e.g. 'follow the text' derives the map's time window from the reader's locus); `IStateEffect<T>`/`IEffectRegistry` (a controller addition) is the async side of that — fetching/JS-interop work an atom's value implies, claimed by one owner at a time so a stale, disposed component can never keep firing effects against a shared atom.
files.l3: Five laws bind every implementation, each with its own property-tested suite in `client.Tests/State/`: (1) single-writer — only `Dispatch` can change `Value`; (2) idempotence — dispatching the same intent twice equals dispatching it once; (3) no-echo — a link-derived update carries its deriving link's name as `Origin`, and a bidirectional link pair must never re-derive back through its own source (see `StateLinkRunner`'s own doc comment for the concrete mechanism); (4) confluence — the same intent sequence yields the same final state regardless of render timing; (5) agreement — every projection of one atom is equal at every instant (trivially true by construction once `IProjection<T>` never stores its own copy). `AtomNames` (line ~148) is the one closed vocabulary of atom name strings (`locus`, `time-window`, `focus-stack`, `selection`, `view-arrangement`) — extend-only, reflected over by `client.Tests`' own conformance test for atom registration. `IStateEffect<T>` was a CONTROLLER ADDITION (2026-08-26) retiring two real defect classes ST-2 hit live: stale-instance effects against a shared atom, and a blank-on-remount when the atom was already converged (idempotence means no `Changed` fires for a reconnecting component).

files.role: The one concrete IStateAtom<T> — every named atom in the app is an instance of this class.
files.l1: This is the actual box every shared fact (the current chapter, the current time window) lives inside. Every one of the app's five shared atoms is literally the same class, just constructed with a different name and starting value — there is no per-fact bespoke storage class anywhere.
files.l2: `StateAtom<T>` stores `Value` with a **private** setter — `Dispatch(IIntent<T>)` is therefore the only code path in the whole assembly that can ever change it (law 1, single-writer). `Dispatch` calls the intent's `Apply(Value)`, compares the result against the current value via an injected (or default) `IEqualityComparer<T>`, and silently no-ops — no `Changed`, no `LastOrigin` update — when they're equal (law 2, idempotence). `LastOrigin` records whether the last real change was user-originated (`null`) or link-derived (the deriving link's name), which `StateLinkRunner` reads to avoid oscillation (law 3).
files.l3: `where T : notnull` is the cheap half of an immutability obligation this type can enforce mechanically — law 1 only actually holds if every `T` is an immutable record with `init`-only members (`Locus`, `TimeWindow`, …); a `T` with settable properties would let any holder of `atom.Value` mutate shared state from outside `Dispatch`, silently. `client.Tests/State/StateAtomLawTests.cs` asserts via reflection that `Value` genuinely has no public setter, so a future edit that widens it fails loudly. Registered as a DI singleton per named atom in `Program.cs`/`AppServices.cs` — Blazor WebAssembly has one DI scope for the app's whole life, so singleton lifetime is exactly what a shared, cross-page atom needs.

files.role: The imperative half of a StateLink: subscribes to Source, dispatches derived intents into Target.
files.l1: This is what actually makes a 'link' between two shared facts do something — for example, when the reader's current chapter changes, this is the code that notices and pushes the matching scripture-mode window onto the map's shared state, but only while the 'follow' mode is switched on.
files.l2: `StateLinkRunner<A,B>` takes a `name`, an `IStateLink<A,B>` (the pure declaration of `Derive`/`Active`), and the concrete `StateAtom<A>` Source/`StateAtom<B>` Target. It subscribes to `Source.Changed`; on each fire, if the link is `Active` and `Source.LastOrigin` is `null` (a genuine user gesture, not an echo), it computes `Derive(Source.Value, Target.Value)` and dispatches it into `Target` wrapped in a `LinkDerivedIntent<B>` stamped with this runner's own `name` as `Origin`. `SyncNow()` forces one derive-and-dispatch pass immediately (used when a link's own `Active` flag flips on, so the target re-syncs without waiting for the next unrelated Source mutation).
files.l3: The no-echo guard (`_source.LastOrigin is not null` → skip) is the whole mechanism law 3 needs: a two-link bidirectional pair (Link('ab', A→B) and Link('ba', B→A)) stops oscillating after exactly one hop, because step 2's dispatch into B stamps Origin='ab', and Runner('ba') (subscribed to B.Changed) sees that non-null Origin and refuses to derive back into A. The file's own header discloses a real, deliberate scope limit: `LastOrigin` is STICKY (only updated on an effective change), not momentary, so the guard reads 'was the source's last effective change link-derived', which is sufficient for this app's only real topology (Locus→TimeWindow, one hop) but would need a sharper edge (an Origin carried on the notification itself, not read back off sticky atom state) if a future link chain (A→B→C) is ever added. World.razor's `_followLink`/`_followRunner` is the one real production instance.

files.role: One popover session's whole state as one atom value: the Stack (where back goes) plus the Trail (where you've been).
files.l1: This holds everything one open popover 'session' needs to remember: the breadcrumb stack (so the Back button works) and the full trail of every node you've visited this session (so 'save this exploration' can snapshot the whole journey). It exists as one shared atom so more than one popover instance (the reader's, the map's, the hamburger menu's) can hand ownership of 'the active session' to whichever one is currently open.
files.l2: `FocusStack(IReadOnlyList<Focus> Stack, IReadOnlyList<ExplorationDescriptor> Trail)` is a record with hand-rolled equality comparing `Stack` by each entry's `Descriptor` only (never the live `Node`, which is payload and can differ in identity between two reconstructions of an equal node). Five intents mutate it: `Visit` (push, idempotent — re-visiting the current top is a no-op), `Back` (pop, recording the landed-on node into the trail too — 'a Back landing is a visit'), `Reseed` (restore a full session snapshot verbatim, used when a superseded instance reclaims ownership), `Reset` (close — both stack and trail wiped), and `SeedFromTrail` (rebuild a whole session from an ordered node list, used by the hamburger panel's 'Continue').
files.l3: The hand-rolled `Equals` (descriptor-only) exists because a naive `Stack.SequenceEqual` would only recognize 'no change' when every entry is the literal same node object — which `SeedFromTrail` breaks, since 'Continue' reconstructs fresh node instances via `ExplorationDescriptor.Reconstruct` on every click; two re-seeds of an equal trail would otherwise never compare equal, firing spurious `Changed` events and violating law 2. A documented consequence: because equality is descriptor-only, a law-2 no-op re-seed keeps the atom's already-stored `Focus.Node` instances rather than swapping in the freshly-reconstructed ones — benign today since no code compares node references, but worth knowing. `ExplorerPopover.razor` is the sole real consumer, claiming ownership via `OwnershipRegistry` on mount and releasing on dispose.

files.role: The one concrete IEffectRegistry: claim-on-mount/release-on-dispose ownership of an atom's async materialization.
files.l1: This makes sure that when a shared fact changes (like the map's time window), exactly one currently-alive component is responsible for actually fetching new data because of it — never zero (a stale blank screen) and never two at once racing each other. Whoever 'claims' an effect last wins, and claiming immediately re-runs the effect so nothing goes stale.
files.l2: `EffectRegistry.Claim<T>(IStateEffect<T> effect)` mints a fresh private token as the effect name's current owner, subscribes a handler to `effect.Source.Changed` that only actually materializes when its own token still matches the slot's current owner (so a superseded claimant's handler stays technically wired but permanently inert), and immediately runs `Materialize` against the atom's *current* value if `AppliesTo` says so — this reconcile-on-claim step is what fixes the 'new component mounts, atom is already converged, so no Changed ever fires' blank-pane bug. Releasing (via disposing the returned `EffectClaim`) unsubscribes and clears ownership if this claim is still current.
files.l3: The supersession mechanism is a plain `object` token compared by reference — not subscription membership — which is what makes 'latest wins' correct independent of Blazor's own undocumented dispose-vs-mount ordering (the exact hazard a prior batch's review named as the reason a per-handler boolean guard doesn't scale). A fix round added a proactive `Unsubscribe` field so a superseded claimant's handler is detached immediately rather than staying wired-but-inert until its own eventual Dispose — cheap hardening on top of the token check, which alone already made this correct. `Release(name)` (a separate public method) lets a caller about to write directly to an atom release whoever currently owns that effect name, by name, without needing to know whether it itself is the owner — closing a gap where the original per-instance `Dispose` couldn't release someone else's still-active claim. `DelegateEffect<T>` (line ~220) is a small adapter so a call site can declare an effect as three plain values instead of hand-writing a bespoke `IStateEffect<T>` class. Blazor WebAssembly is single-threaded, so the backing `Dictionary<string, Slot>` needs no locking. Covered by `client.Tests/State/EffectRegistryTests.cs`, including a `TwoRapidReClaims...` test proving the dispose-then-sync-then-claim ordering closes a real double-materialize window.

files.l1: A small helper that lets two different list objects with the same items in the same order count as 'equal' for state-atom purposes. files.role: The one reset-on-fault async-memoization idiom every 'one shared fetch per node instance' class uses.
files.l1: A small helper that makes sure a node only ever fetches its own data once, no matter how many parts of its popover ask for it at the same moment — and if that one fetch fails, the next attempt tries again fresh instead of staying permanently broken.
files.l2: `AsyncMemo<T>.Get(Func<Task<T>> fetch)` caches the in-flight or completed `Task<T>` itself, not the resolved value — assigned synchronously, before any `await` resolves, so a second concurrent caller sees the same pending task and awaits it rather than starting a new HTTP request. `CompletedValueOrDefault` reads the already-resolved value without ever blocking, for the rare case a node needs a synchronous peek (e.g. `EventNode.CachedKind`).
files.l3: The fault-handling is the whole point: a naive task-memoizing cache without reset-on-fault would permanently poison a node instance after one transient network failure — a real regression from the pre-existing value-memoizing `_cached ??= await ...` idiom, which self-healed on the next call since it only ever assigned on success. `ObserveFault` (an `async void` fire-and-forget watcher — one of the few legitimate uses of that pattern) clears `_task` only if it still holds the exact instance that faulted (`ReferenceEquals`), so a caller that already retried and installed a newer task is never clobbered. The class's own doc comment records a genuine ordering bug its first draft had: assigning the field inside an `async` continuation resets it BEFORE the caller has even assigned it, whenever the fetch faults synchronously — fixed by assigning first, then observing. Used by six-plus node classes (VerseNode, PassageNode, EventNode, PlaceNode, CatechismNode, ChapterNode, and CompositionSplit) that discovered the same live race under `ExplorerPopover.LoadCurrent`'s concurrent `Task.WhenAll` dispatch — GEN.1.1 was measured firing six concurrent, identical `/api/verse/{vref}` requests before this fix. Covered by `client.Tests/Explore/AsyncMemoTests.cs`, including `AFaultedFetchResetsTheCache`, the test that caught the ordering bug.

files.role: The maximal-run grouping algorithm: which consecutive verses in a list count as one 'passage.'
files.l1: This is the rule for when several verses next to each other should render as one flowing passage instead of separate verse rows — used by every verse-list surface in the app (cross-references, THE SCRIPTURES, place dates) so they all agree on what counts as a passage.

files.role: PassageBlockBuilder: turns one or more verse-lists into renderable, truncation-honest passage blocks, with gap-aware coalescing.
files.l1: This is the engine behind every scrollable list of verses in the app — it takes raw verse text and groups it into readable passages, and it is honest about truncation: if the server only sent the first 20 verses of a long chapter, this shows '+N more' rather than silently pretending that's everything. Its trickiest job is handling a Gospel account that genuinely skips around (like Peter's denial, told across two separate verse ranges) without inventing verses that don't exist.
files.l2: `PassageListVerse(Vref, Text, GroupCount?, Places?, Persons?, WordsOfChrist?)` is the common currency every verse-list surface hands in. `PassageSourceUnit` is one independent source of verses (e.g. one cross-reference target's own member verses); grouping never merges across two different units even if their verses are numerically adjacent. `PassageBlockBuilder.Build(units)` returns `List<PassageBlockData>` — for an ordinary unit it delegates straight to `PassageGrouping.Groups`; for a unit marked `CoalesceAcrossChapters` (an event witness account), it calls `BuildCoalescedBlock` instead, which can span chapter boundaries but never fabricates a bridge over a real gap. `VerseTextResolver.ResolveAsync`/`ResolveGroupsAsync` resolve full KJV text for an already-known verse-ref list via the existing chapter fetch + LRU cache.
files.l3: `BuildCoalescedBlock`'s three-step algorithm (documented at length in the file, ACCT-COALESCE-1, fix rounds 1-3): (1) `TrueRunsOf` splits delivered verses into single-chapter runs, correcting each run's own true end for the server's 20-verse-per-chapter cap (the cap always keeps the LOWEST-numbered verses, so an undelivered remainder continues after the last delivered one — clamped to the chapter's own real length via `Versification`, never inventing verses past the chapter's end); (2) `StitchRuns` merges adjacent runs across a chapter boundary ONLY where `Versification` proves the prior chapter's own true last verse and the next run opens at verse 1 of the very next chapter (Sermon on the Mount's MAT.5-7 genuinely joins; Peter's denial's MRK.14.54 + 66-72 genuinely does not); (3) `AccountSpan` renders the honest, possibly-compound ref text ('MRK.14.54, 66-72'), never a fabricated envelope. `PassageBlockData.ExploreSref`/`ExploreVerseCount` (fix round 3) exist because a compound/cross-chapter Span string is not parseable by the server's `ScriptureRef::parse` — pushing it verbatim as a PassageNode sref made `/api/xrefs`/`/api/catechism` 400 for 167 of 1212 real accounts before this fix; the account now explores by its own first contiguous same-chapter run instead, with the displayed ref staying the honest compound Span. This file's own doc comments record a multi-round review history (a false premise about 'always contiguous' corrected in fix round 2, a further overrun-clamping fix in round 3). Covered by `client.Tests` (grep for PassageBlock/AccountSpan/BuildCoalescedBlock tests).

files.role: Scans a verse's text for attested place/person name spans — the app's only in-text mention detection.
files.l1: This is what turns plain verse text into clickable spans over the exact words 'Jerusalem' or 'Aaron' when they appear in a verse the graph already knows mentions that place or person. It's a literal, case-sensitive text search, not a smart language model — it finds only the curated names it's told to look for, and it can miss a pronoun or an old-spelling variant.
files.l2: `MentionSegment(Text, PlaceId?, PlaceName?, PersonId?, PersonName?)` is one slice of scanned text — plain prose, or an attested mention of exactly one kind. `PlaceMentions.Scan(text, places, persons)` finds every occurrence of every candidate name (via `FindAll`, a private word-boundary-checked substring search), then resolves overlaps with a longest-match-wins, stable-sorted acceptance pass (a name that legitimately contains a shorter one, like 'Beersheba' containing 'Sheba', claims the span first).
files.l3: Case-SENSITIVE matching (a deliberate fix from an earlier case-insensitive version) is what distinguishes the place 'Sin' from the common English word 'sin' — every candidate name is already curated/attested, never a raw dictionary lookup, so exact-case matching is a strict precision improvement. `FindAll`'s own word-boundary check (the character immediately before/after a match must not itself be a letter) fixes a real, Playwright-caught bug: a bare substring search found 'Sin' both as EXO.16.1's own genuine mention AND as the first three letters of 'Sinai' later in the same verse. The doc comment discloses a real same-verse ambiguity (GEN.28.1 has both a Place 'Canaan' and a Person 'Canaan' at the identical text position) resolved by a stable sort that happens to prefer the linguistically correct reading there, but is explicitly NOT a claim of real sense-disambiguation. Covered by `client.Tests` (grep for PlaceMentions tests) and `tests/ux/popover-sections.spec.ts`'s MENTION-3 case.

files.role: Resolves a provenance id (e.g. 'kretzmann/genesis') against the fetched Sources document — the fail-loud '?' law.
files.l1: This is what powers the little '?' button next to almost everything in a popover — it turns a raw source-id string into a real, readable attribution ('Sourced from OpenBible', its license, etc). If an id doesn't match anything in the registry, it says so loudly rather than silently showing nothing — a piece of data with no honest source is treated as a bug worth surfacing, not hiding.
files.l2: `ProvenanceResolver.SplitId(id)` splits an id at its first '/' into `(Kind, Locator?)` — the kind is the registry key, the remainder (if any) is this row's own locator. `Resolve(doc, id)` looks up the kind in the already-fetched `SourcesDocumentOut`, returning a `ResolvedProvenance` with one of three `ProvenanceStatus` values: `Resolved`, `Unresolved` (the registry loaded but doesn't contain this id — a DATA fault, shout loud), or `RegistryUnavailable` (`/api/sources` itself failed to load — an INFRASTRUCTURE fault, distinct and gentler). `ResolveAll` resolves a whole section's worth of ids at once, deduplicated by normalized id.
files.l3: The three-status split is a documented fix-round correction: an earlier version treated a failed `/api/sources` fetch identically to a genuinely-unresolvable id, so one dropped network request rendered 'Unrecognized source "kjv". Please report it.' on EVERY affordance on the popover — accusing perfectly well-registered data of having no source. `NormalizeId` collapses null/empty/whitespace to one canonical blank string so several 'nothing to attribute this with' flavors dedupe to ONE loud notice, not several identical ones. A second, documented fix round removed a blank-id FILTER that used to sit at four separate call sites, which had silently made 'a curatorial claim with no attribution' render as nothing at all — the review's own framing: 'no attribution section' and 'an attribution we cannot read' are different facts and must not look the same. `ConfidenceNote` renders nothing for the common 'Imported' confidence level (the app's default register) and a real note for the other three (`CanonicalText`, `Curated`, `Derived`). No dedicated unit test file by name; the fail-loud law is exercised by `tests/ux/provenance.spec.ts`.

files.role: IPopoverSectionContext/IPopoverSectionProvider and PopoverSectionRegistry — the ordered list of every popover section.
files.l1: This is the recipe book that says which pieces of content go into a popover, and in what order — the verse text first, then event membership, then catechism, then parallels, then cross-references last. Each piece knows how to check 'does this node have anything for me to show', and only the pieces that say yes actually render.
files.l2: `IPopoverSectionContext` is `ExplorerPopover`'s own back-channel handed to every provider: `PushAsync` (drill into a new node), `ToggleSelectAsync` (Ctrl/Cmd-click into the tray), `OtherContextSectionCount`/`XrefEntryPoint` (read live at render time, never captured during the concurrent resolve phase), `Graph` (the generic client), and `NavigateWorldAsync` (the map-focus-at-time hand-off). `IPopoverSectionProvider` has two members: `AppliesTo(node)` (cheap, synchronous) and `ResolveAsync(node, api, ctx)` (possibly-fetching, returns `null` for 'no content'). `PopoverSectionRegistry.Providers` is a flat, `Order`-key-sorted list of all 28 registered providers (defined in `PopoverSectionProviders.cs`).
files.l3: `Entries` is an array of `(Provider, int Order)` tuples; `Providers` sorts them once, via `OrderBy` (a documented-stable LINQ sort — two entries sharing an `Order` value resolve in array declaration order, preserving a pre-existing tie-break rule). The doc comment is a running history of the owner's own reordering rulings (FRONTIER-ORDER-1: 'Verse, Event, Catechism, Parallels, then cross references'; CHRONO-MERGE-1 then EVT-META-TOP-1 reordering an Event node's own Chronology vs. date/place blocks) — the Order values (10, 20, 21, 30, 40, 50, 60...210) are deliberately spaced to leave room for future insertions without renumbering everything. A node kind no provider claims at all falls back to that node's own `BodyAsync` (Book/Author/TimeAndPlace remain reached this way today). Adding or removing a provider here is the entire integration surface a new kind of content needs — neither `ExplorerPopover.razor` nor any `IExplorable` node needs to change. files.role: The 28 IPopoverSectionProvider implementations — the actual content behind every popover section.
files.l1: This is the single largest file in the whole client, and it earns it: it holds every single piece of content a popover can show — the verse text with its expand-to-read-the-chapter control, cross-references, THE SMALL CATECHISM, an event's date and place, its parallel Gospel accounts, its chronology arrows, a place's established/destroyed dates, a person's card, and more. Each piece is written as its own small class that answers two questions: 'does this kind of thing have something for me to show' and 'if so, build it.' If you ever wonder 'why does clicking this show that text', the answer is almost certainly a class in this file.
files.l2: Every class implements `IPopoverSectionProvider` (`client/Explore/PopoverSections.cs`): `AppliesTo(node)` checks `node.Kind` (a string switch, e.g. `"Verse" or "Passage"`), and `ResolveAsync(node, api, ctx)` fetches (via the node's own memoized `AsyncMemo`-backed method, e.g. `VerseNode.DetailAsync`) and returns a `PopoverSection?` — `null` means 'nothing to show', which is a real, common, and correct answer, never an empty placeholder. Providers are grouped by which `IExplorable` kind they apply to: `ChapterCardSection`/`YearFrontierSection` (one each, for Chapter/Year); six for Verse/Passage in the owner's ruled order (`VerseTextSectionProvider`, `VerseEventMembershipSection`, `VersePassageMembershipSection`, `CatechismSeamSection`, `VerseParallelsSection`, `CrossRefsSection`); four for Place (`PlaceDescriptionSection`, `PlaceDatesSection`, `PlaceBlurbSection`, `PlaceEventsSection`); four for Catechism items; eight for Event (`EventProvenanceSection` through `EventMentionsSection`); three for PolityDelta; and one each for Person and CommentaryItem. `FrontierProvenance` (an internal static helper class) is the one shared implementation of the section-heading '?' attribution affordance every provider that needs one calls into, rather than nine near-identical copies.
files.l3: The file is dense with disclosed history — most classes' doc comments record which owner ruling shaped their exact content and ordering, and several record real, live-caught bugs their current form fixes: `CrossRefsSection`'s own eager-fetch-first-N-then-lazy-fetch-remainder split exists because eagerly resolving every cross-reference target's chapter (GEN.1.1 has 61) fired dozens of unneeded concurrent requests before a popover even fully opened; `EventChronologySection`'s divergence test (`Diverges`) implements CHRONO-MERGE-1, comparing a narrative leg against the same event's global-timeline leg and rendering a 'story thread' line only for the ~28% of legs that genuinely disagree; `EventAnaloguesSection`/`EventMentionsSection` implement the ATTEST-1 correction that un-conflated 'similar but distinct events' from 'accounts of the same event' after a real leper-healing mixup was reported. `EventMembershipHeading` is the exhaustive, drift-failing kind-to-heading mapping ("event"->"EVENT", "general"->"PASSAGE") `VerseEventMembershipSection`/`VersePassageMembershipSection` both read rather than each hand-rolling a ternary — pinned by `client.Tests/Explore/EventMembershipHeadingTests.cs`. Almost every provider is fail-soft (a try/catch returning `null` on fetch failure, never propagating an exception into the popover's own render). Registration order/priority lives in the sibling file `PopoverSections.cs`, not here — this file is content only. Tested extensively across `client.Tests` (PopoverSectionRegistryTests.cs, EventMembershipHeadingTests.cs) and dozens of `tests/ux/*.spec.ts` Playwright specs (popover-sections, event-timeline, accounts-and-mentions, w1-4-passages).

files.role: The one canonical verse-line renderer: verse number + text + mentions + xref marker, reused everywhere a chapter renders.
files.l1: This is what actually draws one line of Scripture — the verse number, the text with clickable place/person names, and a small superscript letter if the verse has cross-references. Both the main reader page and the popover's own 'read the whole chapter' expansion use this exact same component, so a verse behaves identically wherever it appears.
files.l2: Takes a `VerseOut` plus `Book`/`Chapter`, and a long list of parameters that let two different containers (the full-page reader, and a nested mini-reader inside a popover) customize CSS classes/testids/whether the verse number is a real button (Reader, for shift-click range selection) or a plain span (mini-reader). Clicking the row calls `OnExplore` with a fresh `VerseNode`; Ctrl/Cmd-click calls `OnToggleSelect` instead. Renders `<MentionText>` for the verse's own in-text place/person spans and red-letter wrapping, and an optional `<sup>` xref marker whose click commits and whose hover (main reader only) previews.
files.l3: This component replaced two independent, drifting hand-copies of near-identical verse-rendering markup (Reader.razor's own loop and MiniReaderExpand.razor's own loop) after an owner defect report that a verse clickable in one context did nothing in the other. `ComputeXrefLetters` (a static, pure function both callers call once before their own verse loop, never a mutable counter inside a `foreach`) assigns each xref-bearing verse's ordinal letter via `BijectiveBase26` — spreadsheet-column-style numeration (a, b, ..., z, aa, ab, ..., zz, aaa, ...) chosen specifically because plain modulo-26 wraparound would collide the 27th xref-bearing verse's letter back onto the 1st's, a real risk in a long acrostic psalm like PSA.119. `XrefMarkerAriaLabel` deliberately carries no count language, matching the visual glyph's own owner-mandated 'no count signal at the marker' rule. `OnXrefHoverEnter`/`OnXrefHoverLeave` are deliberately left unwired by MiniReaderExpand — hovering across chapter text one popover deep would unpredictably jump the stack around. Covered by `client.Tests/VerseLineTests.cs` (BijectiveBase26 boundary values) and reader/Kretzmann/popover-sections Playwright specs.

files.role: The one in-text mention-scan-and-render primitive, wrapping red-letter (words-of-Christ) sub-ranges.
files.l1: This is what turns a verse's plain text into text with clickable place/person names inside it, and wraps Jesus's own words in red where the data marks them. It exists because two different files used to each render this exact same thing slightly differently, which is exactly the kind of drift this app's own house rules forbid.
files.l2: `MentionText` takes `Text`, `Places`/`Persons` (attested mentions), and `WordsOfChrist` (red-letter spans). `ComputeRuns` (a pure, static, directly testable method) splits `Text` at the WordsOfChrist char-offset boundaries into an ordered list of red/non-red runs; each run is then handed to `<MentionScan>` (the actual place/person-span rendering loop) independently, wrapped in a `.words-of-christ` span when red. The overwhelmingly common case (no red-letter spans at all) produces exactly one non-red run covering the whole text — byte-identical rendering to before red letters existed.
files.l3: `ComputeRuns` defends against a malformed/out-of-range span (clamped via `Math.Clamp`, never a throw) even though the server's own alignment walk is trusted to hand back sorted, non-overlapping spans. `ClassPrefix` doubles as both the CSS class root and the data-testid root, and callers keep their own pre-existing prefix ('verse-mention' for Reader, 'popover-reader-mention' for the mini-reader, 'popover-passage-mention' for PassageList) so no existing Playwright locator needed to change when this extraction happened. A documented, accepted approximation: a mention name that happens to straddle a red/narration boundary (never observed in real committed data) would not be detected as one whole span in the affected half. Covered by `tests/ux/reader-red-letters.spec.ts`.

files.l1: Whenever a popover shows a list of verses — cross-references, catechism proof verses, place dates — this is the component actually drawing it. It groups consecutive verses into flowing passages instead of separate rows, clamps how much text shows per entry, and offers a 'more / all / less' control when there's more than the initial view.
files.l2: Takes `Units` (a list of `PassageSourceUnit`, from `PassageBlock.cs`), builds `PassageBlockData` blocks via `PassageBlockBuilder.Build`, and renders each as one explorable `<div>` — a captioned entry uses `<TitledPassageEntry>`; every other entry gets a bare ref-label span. files.l1: This is the small '?' button next to almost anything in a popover that tells you where the data came from — click it and a panel opens right there in the flow, naming the source, what it is, its license. It never appears as a floating overlay, and it never opens on hover — only a real click, so it works correctly on a touchscreen too.

files.role: The one place every host page's split-pane machinery lives — role, divider, hatch invocation, URL persistence.
files.l1: This is what actually makes 'the reader and the map side by side' work, for every page that can host a split screen (the reader, the map, Sources, Kretzmann, Concord). Instead of each page building its own split-screen logic, every one of them just wraps its own content in this one component and gets the resize handle, the URL-remembers-the-split behavior, and the close button for free.
files.l2: Takes `HostName`, an optional `SplitModeOverride` (null = self-determine from the shared `ViewArrangement` atom; explicit true = mounted as a registry guest), and a `RenderFragment<CompositionSplitContext>` `ChildContent`. Computes `Composition` (a `IViewComposition`, via `ViewRegistry.ComposeFrom`, memoized for one render pass keyed on the atom value's own reference) and renders one of three branches: an error toast for an unrecognized layout kind, the bare `ChildContent` when not split, or (when this instance is the host) a real `.split-view` flex container with the guest mounted alongside a `<SplitDivider>`. Owns the arrangement atom's `Changed` subscription exactly once — no host page needs its own subscribe/unsubscribe pair.
files.l3: The header comment records three real, self-caught live regressions from earlier revisions, each now load-bearing house law: (a) Blazor's diffing DISCARDS and recreates every DOM node inside `ChildContent` across a single-to-split-h transition (structurally different render trees, not a class change) — a JS watcher that captures a direct DOM reference and binds only on `firstRender` will silently end up bound to an orphaned node, which is exactly what happened to `reader.js`'s `watchChapterNavCenter`; the fix pattern is binding on every render, relying on the JS side being idempotent and self-cleaning; (b) `Nav.NavigateTo` must never be called from a component's own lifecycle synchronous prefix (before the first genuine `await`) — even a same-URL call re-enters Blazor's navigation pipeline and can throw `InvalidOperation_EnumFailedVersion` from inside the framework's own location-changed handling; `SyncSplitUrl`'s own `uri == Nav.Uri` no-op guard is documented as correct today only because every reachable path happens to yield a same-URL no-op, not because the guard makes a different-URL call safe. `SPLIT-PERSIST-1` (RULING 5) owns the whole '?split=&follow=1' URL-projection trio here — restore-once-on-load via `[SupplyParameterFromQuery]`, project-on-change via the owned subscription — so every host gets refresh-survives-split for free. `OnAfterRenderAsync` always attempts a live 50/50 measurement of `.split-view`'s real width on first open (falling back to `ViewArrangement.InitialDividerFraction` only when no stored fraction exists), per an owner order that a split used to open lopsided. Covered by `tests/ux/composition.spec.ts` (including a `page.on('pageerror')` fixture added specifically to catch a hard crash from the orphaned-DOM-reference hazard class) and `client.Tests`' `ConformanceTests.cs` (the `ArrangementStateAssignmentPattern` scan).

files.role: The real, live drag-resize handle for the reader/atlas split, with keyboard nudge and clamped width.
files.l1: This is the thin vertical bar between the reader and the map when they're split — drag it to resize either side, or use the arrow keys while it's focused. It used to be just a static, non-interactive line; this component made it a real, working resize handle.

Pointer-drag mechanics mirror `TimeSlider.razor`'s established pattern (pointerdown seeds drag-start state; pointermove recomputes a live value; pointerup ends the gesture), extended with `reader.js`'s `capturePointer` since this divider's own hit area is narrow and a drag routinely travels far past it.
files.l3: `EnsureMaxWidthAsync` re-measures `.split-view`'s real content-box width at the START of every gesture (never cached across gestures) via `reader.js`'s `getPaneRect`, so a browser resize between two separate drags is always correctly accounted for; a failed measurement degrades to `double.MaxValue` (no clamp for that one gesture) rather than blocking the drag. `DividerWidthPx` (13px, matching app.css's own fixed hit-area width exactly) is subtracted from the clamp math — without it, a real, live-caught discrepancy silently shorted the atlas pane's own floor by exactly that amount (320 became 307). `_lastDraggedWidthPx` (not the `WidthPx` parameter) is what `OnPointerUp` reports, since Blazor parameter updates only land on the next render and reading `WidthPx` from inside the same synchronous pointer-up burst risks a stale value. files.role: The parchment hover card floating over the map — verse content, dates, blurb, narrative adjacency — self-placing.
files.l1: This is the card that pops up when you hover (or click-pin) a place on the map. It shows the place's name, the verses that mention it grouped into readable passages, a short historical blurb when one exists, and its established/destroyed dates — and it figures out on its own whether to appear above or below the marker so it never gets cut off by the edge of the screen.
files.l2: Takes `Place` (a `ScenePlace`), `X`/`Y` (the marker's screen anchor point), `WindowFrom`/`WindowTo`, and a set of callbacks (`OnOpenPlace`, `OnExploreNode`, `OnGoToPlace`, `OnClosePin`). `MergedVerses()` flattens every shown event's own verse groups into one deduped, canonically-ordered list; `Groups()`/`VisibleGroups()` (delegating to `PassageGrouping`) split that into passage/lone-verse blocks, revealed incrementally via `_shownCount` (4 initially if the first group is a passage, 2 if it's a lone verse, growing by 5 or 2 per 'more' click). `LoadHistory`/`LoadNarrativePositions` lazily fetch the blurb/dates and narrative prior/next adjacency once the card actually opens.
files.l3: Self-placement (a HOTFIX-batch feature) is a deliberate SNAPSHOT decision, not continuously tracked: `OnAfterRenderAsync` measures this card's own rendered box (`MapInterop.MeasureCardPlacement`) exactly once per genuinely new place, and only after BOTH the chapter-text and history fetches have settled (`_contentReady`) — measuring earlier would size against not-yet-loaded, conditionally-present sections. `CardPlacement.Compute` (a standalone, unit-tested pure function, not a method here) decides flip-above-vs-below AND a pixel clamp adjustment on whichever edge still overflows even after flipping — a documented fix-round correction closed a real bug where a flipped card was never checked against the container's own bottom edge (a 122px overflow, live-reproduced). Because World.razor renders this with no `@key`, hovering from one marker straight to another reuses the SAME component instance with a new `Place` parameter — `_lastPlaceId`'s guard in `OnParametersSetAsync` is what resets expand/verse-text state for the new place rather than showing the previous place's already-fetched text. `NarrativeRows()` derives prev/next event adjacency from `LoadNarrativePositions`'s own unwindowed `positions_for_events` resolver — a documented fix retiring an earlier, windowed `Arrows`-parameter derivation the review proved could disagree with the verse popover's own positions for an entirely ordinary time-slider window. Covered extensively by `tests/ux/world*.spec.ts` and `world-hover-text.spec.ts`'s own black-box mirror of `MergedVerses`.

files.role: The one prior/following arrow-traversal component — dwell-hover verse peek, chronological refs, inline story-thread mode.
files.l1: This draws the little prior/next arrows that let you walk backward and forward through an event's own chronological position — click to jump, or hold your pointer over one for a moment to peek at its verses without leaving the current popover. It's used both for the big block-style arrows and for a small inline arrow inside a sentence when a narrative's own story genuinely diverges from plain chronology.
files.l2: Takes `Direction` ('prior'/'following'), `Adjacent` (the target event, or null for a chain end), `Glyph`, and `Inline`/`InlinePrefixText` (the two rendering modes). A real component (not a static render-helper) specifically because the dwell-hover peek needs a timer that outlives one render — `OnPointerEnter` starts a fresh `CancellationTokenSource` timer (`DwellTiming.PeekDelayMs`, ~375ms); if the pointer leaves before it fires, the peek never shows. `Commit` (click) is wired completely independently of the dwell timer — a genuine click always commits immediately regardless of peek state. `RefDescriptors`/`SelectRefs`/`SelectRefsFromWitnesses` render the adjacent event's account refs (never verse text) via `<RefsList>`, per an owner ruling that chronological traversal shows 'the list of refs', not verse contents.
files.l3: `SelectRefsFromWitnesses` (fix round 2, ACCT-SET-MISMATCH-1) fixes a real, owner-reported bug: the narrative-endpoint's own `VerseGroups` field is not guaranteed to carry EVERY witness of an event (a real curated event had two witnesses, but the endpoint's own derivation only carried one) — this method eagerly fetches the adjacent event's full `EventDetail.Witnesses` and derives refs the IDENTICAL way `WitnessUnitsResolver` does for the landed frontier's own PARALLEL ACCOUNTS, so the set AND order shown under the arrow always matches what clicking through actually reveals — `SelectRefs` (the older, flatter `VerseGroups`-based derivation) is now only a fallback used until that fetch resolves. The dwell-peek's own placement math (`OnAfterRenderAsync`) measures against the enclosing `.popover`'s own real clipping boundary, not the viewport — a fix-round correction after a reviewer live-reproduced a many-verse peek spilling ~269px past the popover's own bottom edge when budgeted against `window.innerHeight` instead. `ScheduleDismiss`/`CancelDismiss` give the pointer a ~1000ms grace period to travel across the small visual gap between the arrow and an already-open peek box, reusing the exact tuned figure Reader.razor's own xref marker-to-panel transit already proved correct, rather than re-deriving a smaller number and risking rediscovering the same race. files.role: A small, fixed-capacity least-recently-used cache — the generic building block AtlasClient's per-endpoint caches use.
files.l1: A simple 'remember the last N things' cache — when it's full and something new comes in, it forgets whichever entry hasn't been touched in the longest time. AtlasClient uses several of these, one per kind of data, so recently-viewed chapters and scenes reload instantly.
files.l2: `LruCache<TKey, TValue>(capacity)` — `TryGet(key, out value)` returns a hit and marks the entry as most-recently-used; `Put(key, value)` inserts or refreshes an entry, evicting the least-recently-used one if a genuinely new key would exceed capacity. Backed by a `Dictionary` (O(1) lookup) plus a `LinkedList` (O(1) move-to-front/remove-last) — the standard LRU data-structure pairing.
files.l3: Not thread-safe, by design — the Blazor WASM runtime this backs is single-threaded, so no locking is added. Every field/method is generic over `TKey`/`TValue`, with `where TKey : notnull` matching `Dictionary`'s own constraint. No dedicated unit test file found by name; its eviction correctness is implied by `AtlasClient`'s own caching behavior working correctly across the app's test suite.

files.role: The app-lifetime singleton backing the hamburger menu's saved-explorations list — localStorage-backed.
files.l1: This is what remembers every exploration you've saved — snapshotting the current trail under an auto-generated name, letting you rename or delete a saved one, and persisting the whole list to the browser's storage so it survives a reload.
files.l2: `SavedExploration(Id, Name, CreatedUtc, Nodes)` is one saved entry. `SavedExplorationsService` restores its list once at construction (via `LocalStore.Read`), and `Save`/`Rename`/`Delete` each mutate `_items` then call `Persist()` (write-through plus raising `Changed`). `Available` (the cached result of `LocalStore.Probe`) is what the hamburger button and the popover's own save button both read to decide whether to render at all.
files.l3: `Changed` (a plain C# event, not a state atom) exists specifically because this service is injected into multiple independent component instances at once (the popover's save button; the hamburger panel's list) — a mutation made from one must tell the other to re-render, the same 'one owner mutates, every reader re-renders on notice' shape `NavigationManager.LocationChanged` already gives `MainLayout` for route changes. `Save` never mutates a prior entry — 'save = snapshot, not a live link' — each call appends a brand-new entry even if the trail is a superset of a previous save. No dedicated unit test file; exercised via saved-exploration Playwright specs.

files.role: The exact, zero-year-aware year<->pixel math backing the time slider's every drag/click/handle position.
files.l1: This is the pure math behind the time slider — given a year, where on the strip should the handle sit; given a pixel position, what year does that correspond to. It correctly handles the fact that there is no 'year 0' in this calendar (1 BC is immediately followed by AD 1), and it makes sure every short era (like the Exile) still gets a usable, clickable width even though it spans far fewer years than the Bronze Age does.
files.l2: `YearToX(year, eras, width)`/`XToYear(x, eras, width)` are the two round-trip conversions. `EraWidths(eras, width)` computes each era's own segment width: proportional to its year span, but floored at `width / (eras.Count * 2)` so a short era never collapses to an unusable sliver — an iterative re-sharing pass (pin any era whose fair share would fall under the floor, then re-share the remaining width among the rest) ensures the returned widths sum to exactly `width`. `YearToLocalIndex`/`LocalIndexToYear` handle the year-zero skip within one era.
files.l3: `EraWidths` was promoted from private to PUBLIC by a fix round after `TimeSlider.razor`'s own CSS flex-grow-with-min-width-percentage rendering was proven, by an exhaustive era-click property test, to drift from this method's own pixel math — flexbox's min-width-then-proportional-remainder algorithm is a genuinely different resolution procedure, and the drift was large enough at a smaller track width to put a released handle on the NEXT era's own clickable center. `TimeSlider.razor` now calls this directly and renders each band at an exact fixed pixel width, making the visual band and the handle math the SAME numbers by construction. `Epsilon` (1e-7) is reserved off each era's right edge purely so two adjacent eras' own year positions never collide at the shared boundary pixel — without it, `YearToX` would stop being injective and `XToYear` couldn't invert it. Fully covered by `client.Tests/SliderScaleTests.cs`, exercised at a third track width entirely to prove the algorithm never silently hardcoded a specific pixel constant.

files.role: A lightweight, in-memory, app-lifetime singleton remembering where the reader and the atlas were each last left.
files.l1: This remembers, purely in memory (not saved across a hard refresh), where the map camera was pointing and which chapter you were reading, so navigating away and back — including opening and closing a split screen — restores where you left off. It's two independent halves: 'the atlas's last position' and 'the reader's last position', deliberately not coupled to each other.
files.l2: `MapViewState` (camera lat/lon/zoom, the time window or scripture ref, `Follow`, `DividerFraction`) and `ReaderViewState` (Book/Chapter/ScrollY), each with a `HasData` flag distinguishing 'never visited this session' from 'visited and genuinely left sitting here.' `MountReaderChapter`/`UnmountReaderChapter`/`IsReaderChapterMounted` are a reference-counted multiset — separate from `ReaderViewState` — tracking whether a reading surface is ACTIVELY showing a given chapter RIGHT NOW, since two simultaneous reading surfaces (Reader.razor and Kretzmann.razor, following the same chapter in a split) can legitimately both be 'mounted' on it at once.
files.l3: The reference-counted multiset (not a single nullable `(Book, Chapter)?`, and not a plain `HashSet`) is a documented fix-round correction: a single last-writer-wins value was wrong for two reasons — while released, the two split panes can legitimately show DIFFERENT chapters, and a plain non-counted set would let one pane's own disposal wrongly unmount a chapter the OTHER pane is still genuinely showing. Mounting is scoped to a genuinely SUCCESSFUL chapter load only, and the previous chapter this SAME instance had mounted is unmounted before the new fetch starts, keyed off that instance's own last-loaded book/chapter rather than the navigation target, so an instance never leaks a stale 'still mounted' count regardless of whether the new navigation succeeds or fails. Registered as an `AddSingleton` in Program.cs (Blazor WASM has one DI scope for the app's life). No dedicated unit test file for the service itself; its correctness is load-bearing for `MiniReaderExpand`'s own 'already reading this chapter' affordance hiding correctly, tested via popover-sections Playwright specs.

files.role: Formats and parses years/ranges in the exact CONTRACT text format ('1447 BC – 1400 BC'), with no year zero.
files.l1: This turns a plain integer year into the exact text the app always shows ('1447 BC' or 'AD 30'), and a range into 'from – to' with a proper dash — and it knows how to parse that text back into numbers too, for the picker's own manual year-range input box.
files.l2: `Format(year)` returns '{n} BC' for negative years, 'AD {n}' otherwise. `FormatRange(from, to)` joins two formatted years with a spaced EN DASH (U+2013), collapsing to a single year when `from == to`. `FormatClaim(from, to, note)` prefixes 'c. ' when a curated qualifying note is present (e.g. 'traditional'). `TryParse(text, out from, out to)` is the inverse — accepts either the canonical en-dash separator or a plain hyphen (what a keyboard actually types), and rejects '0 BC', unmarked bare digits, and an inverted range.
files.l3: There is deliberately no year zero in this calendar (1 BC is immediately followed by AD 1) — `TryParse` rejects it explicitly rather than silently accepting a meaningless value. Mirrors `tests/ux/lib/years.ts`'s own `formatYear`/`formatRange` functions so the TypeScript property-test helpers and this C# implementation always agree on wire text — two independent implementations of the identical phrase, the same discipline the AQC's own Gherkin corpus uses for contract behavior. Shared by `PlaceCard`'s own instrument-face line and `YearNode`'s own popover title, so the two always read identically for the same underlying claim. No dedicated client.Tests unit file found by name for this class specifically (its formatting is pinned indirectly by every consumer's own coverage and the parallel TypeScript helper).

files.role: The app's one stylesheet — every design token and component rule, one class per rule, no cascading selectors.
files.l1: This is every visual style in the whole app — colors, fonts, spacing, animations — in one file. It follows a strict house rule: every rule targets exactly one class, never a combination of two classes or a parent-child selector, so styling one thing can never accidentally affect something else that happens to share a class.
files.l2: Opens with a `:root` block of CSS custom properties (design tokens) for the two visual materials the app uses — parchment (the reading pages, by day) and dusk (the map, by lamplight) — colors like `--parchment`, `--ink`, `--dusk-deep`, `--ember` (the map marker's glow color), and `--bronze-ink` (a contrast-corrected bronze specifically chosen to clear WCAG AA for small text, since the plain `--bronze` token measures under the 4.5:1 floor). Every component's own CSS lives in its own block further down, one selector per class.
files.l3: The file's own header states the discipline explicitly: 'no chained/descendant selectors, no !important... contextual theming is done with CSS custom properties set by a theme class and inherited down, never by combining two classes in one selector.' Individual token comments carry their own measured-contrast history (e.g. `--bronze-ink`'s own note explains it was introduced specifically because plain `--bronze` text on parchment measured 4.38:1, just under AA) and marker-color tuning history (`--ember` replaced an earlier, too-faint `--lamp-core`-derived color after direct user feedback that markers were 'not cool and glowy'). Loaded by `wwwroot/index.html`. No dedicated tests; visual correctness is implied by every Playwright spec's own screenshot/selector assertions and by accessibility-contrast notes recorded directly in the token comments.
